extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature (scientists, researchers, and informed public)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance and editorial notes embodied in book reviews, letters, and short scientific correspondence published in a research journal; covers expectations for submissions, experimental evidence, nomenclature, and qualities of expository/scientific works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor submission policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Editor does not hold himself responsible for opinions expressed by his correspondents. Neither can he undertake to return, or to correspond with the writers of, rejected manuscripts intended for this or any other part of Nature. No notice is taken of anonymous communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manuscripts and letters submitted to the journal should be signed and should not expect individualized correspondence or return of rejected material; authors bear responsibility for opinions expressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference compilation usefulness and organization
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of the publication is 'to permit astronomers of every class to learn readily what is being done in their own line of work, and by whom and where it is being done, and the arrangement of the matter makes this a very simple task.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A useful reference compilation should be well arranged (e.g., alphabetical lists), comprehensive (observatory country, latitude, longitude, altitude, publications, staff, history, instruments), include society/publication lists, name indices with page references, geographical indexes, and an overall chart showing distributions to assist practical planning (e.g., founding new observatories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience suitability and pedagogical relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: The volume is intended for the Fortbildungsschulen (continuation schools) and contains literary and patriotic sections in addition to the purely technical matter; the purely agricultural part is distinctly practical and contains useful hints on the management of farm stock together with accounts of soils, crops and manures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational works should be tailored to the intended audience (age, level, institutional context), balance motivational/literary material with practical technical instruction, include pedagogical aids (e.g., proverbs or memory aids), and avoid extraneous topics that dilute core curriculum goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus and avoidance of extraneous material
rubrics_metrics.description: We are not quite clear why the authors should have attempted accounts of apparently extraneous matters like the metallurgy of copper and steel, the theory of the microscope and the dynamo. The treatment is necessarily vague and general, and the space might well have been utilised for a fuller development of things falling clearly within the scope of the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should avoid introducing topics outside the defined scope of the work; breadth must not sacrifice sufficient depth — extraneous sections that can only be treated vaguely are better omitted or shifted to more suitable venues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicality and usefulness of technical content
rubrics_metrics.description: The purely agricultural part occupies about a quarter of the volume, and is distinctly practical. Useful hints on the management of farm stock are given, together with general accounts of soils, crops and manures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical sections intended for practitioners or trainees should emphasize actionable, practical guidance and cover the core applied topics expected by that audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific depth and seriousness of theory
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The scientific information is scanty and very elementary. The first half is devoted to 'Généralités et Théories,' but it must be confessed that the theories are not very serious, and that the generalities are the more prominent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works claiming scientific treatment should provide substantive, rigorous theory and not rely mainly on superficial generalities; theoretical sections should be sufficiently developed for the intended scholarly level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and completeness of statistical data and tables
rubrics_metrics.description: A large quantity of statistical information is contained in the last fifteen or twenty pages, in which several tables are given showing the volumes of the various rivers and the numbers of hydro-electric installations. These tables will probably be of more interest to the serious student of the subject than all the rest of the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a book includes empirical/statistical data, the tables should be comprehensive, accurate, and presented so they are directly useful to researchers or serious students; high-quality data can salvage otherwise weak exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposeful use of illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: The illustrations are fairly numerous, and consist chiefly of landscape scenes; they help to make the book appear lighter, but hardly serve any other purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations should serve explanatory or evidentiary purposes rather than merely decorative roles; choose figures that clarify methods, data, or concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental reproducibility and careful methodological reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: By a chemical method this substance was separated from actinium, and a solution of the latter was obtained which showed no appreciable growth of radium over a period of eighty days. Observations on this solution have been continued over a total period of 340 days, and there is still no detectable increase in the quantity of radium. ... Dr. Boltwood has not been able to separate the parent of radium from actinium by the reagent employed by me, viz. ammonium sulphide, but has found the use of sodium thiosulphate effective. In explanation of this discrepancy, he suggests that I employed old ammonium sulphide. As a matter of fact, I did not use the ordinary laboratory solution of ammonium sulphide, but added ammonia to the actinium solution, and then saturated it with sulphuretted hydrogen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should provide enough chemical/experimental detail to allow others to reproduce methods and to explain reagent/preparation differences; long-term observations and careful control of reagent quality must be reported when they affect outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomenclature should be practical, explanatory, and stable
rubrics_metrics.description: Every radio-active substance should be given a name to indicate its position in the scheme of radio-active changes. This system is very excellent in theory, but I have found it extremely difficult to carry out in practice. ... At the same time, I think it will be desirable to retain a distinctive name for those radio-active substances which, like radium, have a long enough life to be separated in sufficient quantity for an examination of properties by the ordinary chemical and physical methods. It is probable that the parent of radium fulfils these conditions, and should thus have a distinctive name like radium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose names that are simple and explanatory where possible; reserve large-scale renaming of systems until the set of known products stabilizes; grant distinctive names to long-lived, separable substances for practical experimental work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design experiments that give decisive, testable predictions
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not intend to discuss more than one point here, for it seems to me that the record of a simple experiment is of more value in deciding between the two hypotheses than a series of comparisons or discussion of probabilities possibly could be. ... I have made experiments to test the two hypotheses, using an electroscope to compare the intensities of secondary radiation as nearly as possible in these two directions. ... These preliminary experiments, however, to my mind furnish quite conclusive evidence in favour of the ether pulse theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simple, well-focused experiments that yield clear, quantitative contrasts between competing hypotheses; derive expected numerical ratios/patterns from each hypothesis and design measurements to distinguish them without unnecessary complication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analysis: report measures, interpret with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief charge made ... was that we had overlooked a curved regression line between magnitude and parallax — that now appears to have disappeared into limbo. ... I agree with Mr. Hinks that this is a point of 'general interest,' and I am glad that his last letter enables me to assert it, not as 'the vaguest of suggestions' ... but as a fact which may be slightly modified when more data are reduced, but is substantially correct as I have given it. ... The colour and magnitude correlation is essentially that determined by Miss Gibson, 0·3: the values for the spectral class and magnitude correlations run up according to the classification used to double this value, and even to 0·7. Meanwhile, the magnitude and parallax relation in its best determination is 0·45.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit numeric measures (e.g., correlation coefficients), be transparent about methods and classifications that affect statistics, beware of over-interpreting suggestive patterns, and allow for modification as more data are collected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and representativeness of experimental materials (limits of inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mendelian experimenter has practically limited himself to the materials so created. He himself chooses for his experiments, and can choose, only glaring differences. In other words, he has, qua experimenter, absolutely no acquaintance with the small differences (fluctuations) which normally distinguish mating individuals in natural breeding. He judges the normal from the abnormal, the rule from the exception, and then appeals to earth to note the precision of his methods and thanks heaven he is not as other men, even as mere observers who seek to take the whole of the facts into consideration. If Mendelism deals with any other problem but that of sex, what is that problem? If no other problem can be named, what is the evidence that Mendelism deals with anything more than those abnormalities of sexual reproduction which occur under conditions of artificial selection?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing experiments and drawing conclusions, authors must consider whether their experimental materials and selection procedures are representative of natural conditions; avoid generalizing from artificially selected, extreme materials to broad claims about natural inheritance or processes without supporting evidence.
